subtitle: How a Chishti saint’s rough village tongue became a river of song

panels.shot: wide, dusk-lit view of Baba Farid seated on a simple mat by the Sutlej, silhouettes of villagers listening as fields stretch into haze
panels.action: Baba Farid Ganj-i-Shakar sits cross-legged near a riverbank, eyes half-closed, lips parted in verse, while men and women in rustic dress gather around in rapt silence against the vast Punjab plain.

dialogue.text: In an age of Persian courts and Arabic law, Baba Farid of Ajodhan let the villages speak—and his rough-hewn couplets still echo in scripture centuries later.

i18n.hi: फ़ारसी दरबारों और अरबी क़ानून के दौर में, अजोधन के बाबा फ़रीद ने गाँवों को बोलने दिया—उनके खुरदरे दोहे सदियों बाद भी शास्त्रों में गूंजते हैं।

panels.shot: slow push-in from high above a caravan road between Multan and Delhi, fading into a close on Farid walking with a staff
panels.action: On a dusty road linking Multan to the Gangetic plain, Baba Farid walks with a wooden staff, simple woolen robe and weathered face, passing traders and travelers under a hot sun.

dialogue.text: Farid-ud-Din Masud, later called Ganj-i-Shakar, lived between worlds—Multan’s Sufi circles, Hansi’s teachers, and the long road to Ajodhan in the thirteenth-century Delhi Sultanate.

i18n.hi: फ़रीद-उद-दीन मसूद, जिसे बाद में गंज-ए-शकर कहा गया, दो जहाँ के बीच जीए—मुल्तान की सूफ़ी महफ़िलें, हांसी के उस्ताद, और तेरहवीं सदी के दिल्ली सल्तनत में अजोधन की लंबी राह।

panels.shot: interior medium shot in a modest study-room in Multan, low-angle on a young Farid copying Arabic on a palm-leaf or paper
panels.action: A younger Baba Farid sits in a dim room in Multan, carefully tracing Arabic letters by lamplight, shelves lined with a few manuscripts while a murshid’s shadow watches from the doorway.

dialogue.text: Born into a family touched by learning and piety, Farid’s early path ran through Arabic prayers, Persian texts and the disciplined training of the Chishti Sufi order.

i18n.hi: इल्म और दीन से रौशन ख़ानदान में जन्मे, फ़रीद की शुरुआती राह अरबी दुआओं, फ़ारसी किताबों और चिश्ती सूफ़ी सिलसिले की सख़्त मज़हबी ट्रेनिंग से गुज़री।

panels.shot: close-up on Farid’s attentive face in a khanqah at Hansi, with an elder Chishti saint in soft focus teaching disciples
panels.action: Inside a simple khanqah at Hansi, Baba Farid sits among other disciples, eyes intent on an elder Chishti master who speaks softly, a clay lamp casting warm light.

dialogue.text: The Siyar al-Auliya and Fawa’id al-Fu’wad remember him as a key link in the Chishti chain—teacher to Nizamuddin Auliya’s generation, shaping ways of devotion more than courts or armies.

i18n.hi: सियारुल औलिया और फ़वायदुल फ़ुवाद उन्हें चिश्ती ज़ंजीर की अहम कड़ी मानते हैं—निज़ामुद्दीन औलिया की नस्ल के उस्ताद, जो दरबारों से ज़्यादा इबादत के तौर-तरीके गढ़ते हैं।

panels.shot: wide shot of Ajodhan/Pakpattan town and surrounding fields, khanqah visible as a humble complex on the edge
panels.action: A sweeping view shows the small town of Ajodhan by the Sutlej, mud-brick houses and green fields, with Baba Farid’s khanqah standing low and open near the outskirts.

dialogue.text: When Farid settled at Ajodhan—later Pakpattan—he chose not a capital, but a river town on the frontier of Punjab, where farmers, traders and wanderers passed in endless streams.

i18n.hi: जब फ़रीद अजोधन—जो बाद में पाकपत्तन बना—में टिके, उन्होंने राजधानी नहीं, बल्कि पंजाब की सरहद पर एक नदी-किनारे कस्बा चुना, जहाँ खेतिहर, सौदागर और मुसाफ़िरों की रेला लगा रहता था।

panels.shot: interior wide of the Pakpattan khanqah courtyard, with cooking hearths and travelers seated in rows eating
panels.action: Inside the Pakpattan khanqah, large clay pots simmer over a hearth as Baba Farid moves among seated travelers and poor villagers sharing a simple meal in long rows.

dialogue.text: The Chishti khanqah at Pakpattan became a house of hospitality—bread and comfort for strangers, a node in the networks of travel that stitched Multan, Lahore and Delhi together.

i18n.hi: पाकपत्तन की चिश्ती ख़ानकाह मेहमाननवाज़ी का घर बनी—अजनबियों के लिए रोटी और सुकून, सफ़र के उन रास्तों की गिरह जो मुल्तान, लाहौर और दिल्ली को जोड़ती थी।

panels.shot: close-up on Farid listening at the doorway to two farmers chatting in a thick local dialect
panels.action: At the doorway, Baba Farid leans on the frame, listening quietly as two farmers in coarse clothes talk animatedly in their local tongue about crops and worries.

dialogue.text: Here Farid measured the pulse of the countryside—their speech rough, mixed with Multani and Punjabi forms, their anxieties far from the polished Persian of sultans and scholars.

i18n.hi: यहीं फ़रीद ने देहात की नब्ज़ टटोली—बोली खुरदरी, मुल्तानी और पंजाबी घुली-मिली, फ़िकरें उन शहंशाहों और उलमा की चमकदार फ़ारसी से बहुत दूर।

panels.shot: medium shot of a teaching circle, Farid addressing villagers and disciples seated on mats
panels.action: Baba Farid sits before a small circle of villagers and disciples on reed mats, raising a hand gently as he begins to speak, faces turned toward him with expectation.

dialogue.speaker: baba_farid
dialogue.text: If their hearts are in this tongue, must not God’s remembrance flow in it too?

i18n.hi: अगर उनके दिल इसी ज़बान में धड़कते हैं, तो क्या ख़ुदा की याद इसी में न बहे?

panels.shot: tight close-up on Farid’s mouth as he recites a couplet, background blurred villagers listening
panels.action: The image focuses closely on Baba Farid’s lips and beard as he recites, faint outlines of villagers in the background, sitting utterly still.

dialogue.text: So the saint began to shape brief couplets in their own speech—short slokas on loss, humility and longing, spoken not in courtly Persian but in the idiom of the fields.

i18n.hi: तो फ़रीद ने उनकी ही बोली में छोटे-छोटे दोहे गढ़ने शुरू किए—जाने-नुक़्सान, नम्रता और तड़प पर संक्षिप्त शलोक, दरबारी फ़ारसी नहीं, खेतों की ज़बान में।

panels.shot: medium shot of a villager wiping eyes, moved by the verse, with Farid serene in the background
panels.action: A middle-aged villager sits cross-legged, hand lifting to wipe his eyes, visibly moved, as Baba Farid continues his verse in the background with calm intensity.

dialogue.text: The words were simple, but the impact deep—daily sorrow turned into prayer, the ache of separation framed as a path back to the Beloved.

i18n.hi: लफ़्ज़ आसान थे, असर गहरा—रोज़मर्रा का ग़म दुआ बन गया, जुदाई की चुभन महबूब तक लौटने की राह बन गई।

panels.shot: interior close-up on a disciple’s hand writing lines on rough paper, Farid’s voice heard off-frame
panels.action: Inside a dim corner room, a young disciple bends over a rough sheet, hand carefully copying Farid’s couplets as the saint’s voice drifts in from the courtyard.

dialogue.text: Some disciples carried these sayings onward, memorizing and noting them down. Not all survive, and the verses we have passed through many mouths and pens before reaching us.

i18n.hi: कुछ मुरीद इन कलामों को साथ ले गए, याद करके और लिखकर। सब बच नहीं पाए; जो अशआर आज हैं, कई ज़बानों और कलमों से गुज़रकर हम तक पहुँचे हैं।

panels.shot: bird’s-eye of pilgrims leaving Pakpattan in different directions, carrying the words with them
panels.action: From above, streams of pilgrims and travelers depart Pakpattan’s khanqah gates onto branching roads, some pausing to repeat snippets of Farid’s verse to companions.

dialogue.text: Along trade routes and pilgrimage paths, Farid’s sayings spread—woven into the oral fabric of Punjab, recited in gatherings far beyond Pakpattan’s mud walls.

i18n.hi: सौदा-कारवाँ और ज़ियारत के रास्तों पर, फ़रीद के बोल फैले—पंजाब की ज़बानी रिवायत में बुने गए, पाकपत्तन की मिट्टी की दीवारों से बहुत दूर महफ़िलों में गूंजते रहे।

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide shot of the Pakpattan khanqah under changing skies, hinting at decades passing
panels.action: The Pakpattan khanqah stands through rain, sun and starry nights, people coming and going in shifting clothes and styles, suggesting years passing in silent sequence.

dialogue.text: Farid died around 1266. After him, the khanqah continued, and the Chishti line moved on—toward Delhi, toward Nizamuddin Auliya, carrying memories of the saint of Ajodhan.

i18n.hi: करीब १२६६ में फ़रीद चले गए। उनके बाद भी ख़ानकाह चलती रही, और चिश्ती सिलसिला आगे बढ़ा—दिल्ली की ओर, निज़ामुद्दीन औलिया की ओर, अजोधन के सूफ़ी की याद साथ लिए।

panels.shot: interior wide of a later Delhi Chishti gathering, with Nizamuddin Auliya teaching, a disciple reciting a Farid verse
panels.action: In a Delhi khanqah decades later, Nizamuddin Auliya sits in teaching posture while a disciple at the edge raises his voice to recite a brief couplet attributed to Baba Farid.

dialogue.text: Chishti chronicles like Hasan Sijzi’s Fawa’id al-Fu’wad place Farid within the living chain—his name and sayings honoured among later saints, his style of tenderness admired.

i18n.hi: चिश्ती तज़्किरे, जैसे हसन सिज्ज़ी का फ़वायदुल फ़ुवाद, फ़रीद को ज़िंदा सिलसिले में रखते हैं—उनका नाम और कलाम बाद के औलिया में मक़बूल, उनकी नर्म मिज़ाज अंदाज़ क़द्र की नज़र से देखा गया।

panels.shot: wide shot of Punjab landscape centuries later, with scattered village gatherings where someone recites an old sloka
panels.action: Centuries later, the Punjab countryside stretches under a soft sky, small groups in different villages sitting in courtyards as elders recite pithy verses to younger listeners.

dialogue.text: Across generations, some of Farid’s verse lived on in oral tradition. Language shifted; dialects changed. Yet certain lines stayed, tied to his name and aura.

i18n.hi: पीढ़ी दर पीढ़ी, फ़रीद के कुछ अशआर ज़बानी रिवायत में बचे रहे। ज़बान बदली; बोलियाँ बदलीं। फिर भी कुछ पंक्तियाँ टिकी रहीं, उनके नाम और रूह से बंधी हुई।

panels.shot: interior close-up of hands of Sikh scribes in the early 1600s writing the Guru Granth Sahib, with a folio showing Farid’s name
panels.action: In an early seventeenth-century scriptorium, Sikh scribes sit cross-legged, carefully ink letters on large folios; one page distinctly begins a section headed with Farid’s verses.

dialogue.text: In 1604, when the Guru Granth Sahib was compiled, a selection of slokas attributed to Farid found a home there—anchoring his voice within Sikh scripture’s vast chorus.

i18n.hi: १६०४ में, जब गुरु ग्रंथ साहिब तैयार हुआ, फ़रीद से मनाए गए कुछ शलोक उसमें जगह पाए—उनकी आवाज़ को सिख ग्रंथ की विशाल धुन में जड़ देते हुए।

panels.shot: extreme close-up on the written lines of a Farid sloka, ink slightly faded, script clear
panels.action: An extreme close view shows written lines of a Farid sloka in Gurmukhi script on aged paper, edges worn but the strokes dark and deliberate.

dialogue.text: Scholars note that these verses show a mix of early Punjabi and Multani elements, shaped by centuries of transmission—not identical to modern standard Punjabi, yet unmistakably of the region.

i18n.hi: उलमा बताते हैं कि ये शलोक शुरुआती पंजाबी और मुल्तानी रंगों का मेल हैं, सदियों की नकल-सुनाई से बने—आज की मानक पंजाबी जैसे नहीं, पर साफ़ तौर पर इसी मिट्टी के।

panels.shot: wide, reverent shot of a contemporary Sikh congregation listening as a Granthi recites Farid’s verses
panels.action: In a modern gurdwara, a Granthi sits by the Guru Granth Sahib, reciting softly while a congregation of men and women sit on the carpet, heads covered, eyes closed in attention.

dialogue.text: Today, Farid’s slokas are still sung as part of daily worship—Sufi-born, preserved in Sikh scripture, a reminder of how devotion can cross institutional and communal lines.

i18n.hi: आज भी फ़रीद के शलोक रोज़ाना की अरदास में गाए जाते हैं—सूफ़ी जनम, सिख ग्रंथ में महफ़ूज़, ये याद दिलाते हैं कि इबादत दीवारों और जमातों से ऊपर जा सकती है।

panels.shot: final contemplative close-up of Farid at Pakpattan at twilight, fields behind him fading into darkness
panels.action: Back at Pakpattan in imagined twilight, Baba Farid sits alone on the earth, gaze turned over darkening fields, his expression gentle, as if listening to distant song.

dialogue.text: Farid did not seek to adorn the courts; he let the mother tongue of his land carry the highest longing—and in that choice, his quiet village words became an enduring river of prayer.

i18n.hi: फ़रीद ने दरबार सजाने नहीं चाहा; उन्होंने अपनी धरती की माँ-बोली को सबसे ऊँची तड़प का वाहक बना दिया—और इसी चुनने से उनके देहाती लफ़्ज़ इबादत की बहती नदी बन गए।

subtitle_i18n.en: How a Chishti saint’s rough village tongue became a river of song
subtitle_i18n.hi: कैसे एक चिश्ती सूफ़ी की खुरदरी देहाती ज़बान गीतों की नदी बनी
